title: One breath, one hiss, and the short a in disguise

slides.heading: A letter that breathes and a letter that hisses
body: chaaw cháang pushes ch out on a burst of breath. Palm up again: this one is supposed to move it.
saaw sôo is a flat hiss with no burst behind it at all — air escaping, not air thrown.
Both are new kinds of sound for you. Every letter you have met so far either hummed or stopped; these two do neither.

slides.heading: Two shapes you have to keep apart
body: ช climbs in one smooth unbroken stroke, with a tail flicking up past the top line.
ซ is the same figure with a notch dented into that climbing stroke — one link of a chain snagged in it — and the same tail above.
The notch is the entire difference. Find it before you read the word, not after.

slides.prompt: ช and ซ differ by one detail. Name it, and say which of the two carries it.

answers: The notch dented into the climbing stroke.
ซ has it. ช runs smooth.

slides.heading: Two vowels that are over before they start
body: ะ is a pair of small hooks written after the consonant, and it clips the vowel short. นะ (ná) is the particle that softens whatever you just said.
ิ is the beret you learned last lesson with its upright flick removed — a quick i, gone before it settles. ซิ (sí) urges someone on: go on, do it.
Short is not a shade of long here. It is a different vowel, and next rule it decides a tone.

slides.heading: ะ in disguise
body: ะ sits after its consonant, so a final consonant arriving behind it has nowhere to stand. Thai solves it by lifting the vowel out of the way: it becomes a single curl, ั, written above the initial.
วัน (wan) is a day. กัน (gan) is together. ดัง (dang) is loud.
Nothing about the sound changed. Only where it is written changed, which is why it is worth learning as one vowel with two spellings rather than as two vowels.

slides.heading: Low class, stopped short
body: A low class letter, a syllable stopped dead, and a short vowel: the pitch jumps to the top of your range.
นะ (ná) is exactly that — ะ is short and nothing follows it, which counts as stopped. So is ซิ (sí).
วัด (wát) is to measure: the same short ั, now sealed dead by ด.
นัก (nák) marks a person who does something as a calling, and it stops on the k-stop of ก.

slides.heading: The same letters, ending live
body: ชาย (chaai) is a man and ชาว (chaao) is the people of a place. Both open on ช, which is low class, and both end on a hum.
Live ending, so the low class live rule applies and they land flat — not high.
One letter, two tones, decided entirely by how the syllable ends. That is the machine you are learning.

slides.prompt: ชาย and ซิ both open on a low class letter. One lands flat and one lands high. Say which is which and name the two things that decide it.

answers: ชาย lands flat: it ends on ย, a hum, so the syllable is live.
ซิ lands high: the vowel is short and nothing follows it, so the syllable is dead.
The ending and the vowel length decide it. The class was the same in both.
